MIDI velocity sets the impact speed of the bachi, from 0.12 m/s to 6 m/s, so a harder stroke comes out shorter, brighter and louder at once instead of only louder. At full Velocity Depth that is 33.6 dB between a ghost stroke and a full blow on an open Don on the ō-daiko, and 39.1 dB on the shime.

Played with hands and wheels

MIDI CC1 lays a palm-sized damping patch on the head and goes on damping while it is held, so a stroke played with the hand down is a muted stroke. The pitch wheel presses the head and bends a stroke that is already ringing, and CC16 and CC17 place each hit around and across the head sample-accurately.

Specifications

The numbers.

Formats
VST3, Audio Unit, Standalone
Platforms
macOS, plus Linux and Windows builds
Playable range
16 notes, C3 to D♯6, being 4 drums by 4 strokes
Host parameters
25; 24 automatable, plus Performer as a persisted non-automatable identity
Resolved head modes
20 per head: 4 axisymmetric and 16 with a circumferential order
Audio demos
27 takes, synthesised by the engine and committed to the repository
Included content
No samples, impulse responses, pretrained weights or third-party preset libraries
Licence
Original code under MIT; JUCE used under its own terms
Downloads & docs

Get Taikor.

Download the nightly build

The development path. The latest successful Nightly run carries one artifact with every instrument, for macOS, Linux and Windows. Artifacts are kept for 14 days and a GitHub account is needed to download them.

Open the Nightly runs ↗

Read the manual

How the instrument works block by block, what it does not model, and the sources behind each modelling decision.

Open the README ↗

Listen to the demos

Twenty-seven committed takes, rendered by continuous integration from this instrument's own shipping engine, so they cannot drift from the code.

Open the audio demos ↗

Browse the source

C++20 and JUCE 8. The original code is under the MIT license; JUCE is used under its own terms.

Open the source ↗
What it does not do

Stated plainly.

Taikor does not model the room, the player's body, the stand, or the far head's radiation into the space behind the drum. It gives the enclosed air stiffness but neither mass, its own resonances nor any loss, and it never rings the bachi itself, which acts only as a force.

Taikor loads no samples, replays no recording, and emulates no particular branded instrument. The demonstration audio is generated by the project's own code.

Physically modelled electric guitar

Electry

Write low-tuned riffs, chord parts and leads from your MIDI keyboard. Electry models an eight-string Drop-E guitar across 22 frets, from E1 to D6.

Get for free or buy

Name your price on Gumroad. Downloads are not yet available.

Articulations & tone

Control the performance.

Strings resonate together, picking varies between strokes, and a modelled fretting hand chooses where each note is played along the neck.

  • Seven playing styles. Sustain, palm mute, hammer-on / pull-off, natural harmonic, pinch harmonic, slide and dead note. Hold a keyswitch briefly or latch the style for a whole phrase.
  • Pick direction. Choose down, up or alternate strokes independently of the playing style. Hold the tremolo keyswitch for automatic repeated picking at an adjustable rate.
  • Bends, vibrato and feedback. Use the pitch wheel for bends, a held keyswitch for vibrato and the modulation wheel to push an amplified note into sustained feedback.
  • Pickups and strings. Choose single-coil or humbucker pickups. Adjust pick position, pick hardness, string age and guitar construction to change the attack and tone.
  • Mono, Stereo or Double. Keep one centred guitar, spread its strings across the stereo field, or use two separately modelled performances, one on each side.
  • Individual string triggers. Hold a chord and repick its strings from MIDI or the on-screen fretboard to add rhythmic patterns and accents.
Workflow

Amps, effects and factory rigs.

Four factory rigs cover a dry guitar, Drop-E metal, muted DI and blues rock lead.

Choose American Clean, British Crunch or Modern High-Gain, then add distortion, compression, delay and room ambience. Set all five effect amounts to zero for a dry signal you can run through your own amp and effect plug-ins.

Circuit-modelled polysynth

YouKnow

Pads, strings, bass and leads from a synth inspired by the Juno-106. YouKnow models its six-voice architecture in software, with the synthesis controls together on one panel.

Get for free or buy

Name your price on Gumroad. Downloads are not yet available.

Synthesis

Oscillators, filter and chorus.

  • Oscillators. Combine saw and pulse waves, add a sub oscillator and blend in noise. Pulse-width modulation adds movement to a held note.
  • Filter and envelope. Shape swells, stabs and sweeps. At full resonance, the filter self-oscillates and becomes a playable tone.
  • Stereo chorus. Choose mode I for a slower swirl, II for faster movement or I+II for a narrower texture. Adjust the hiss separately.
  • Voice character. Unit Character varies the modelled components between voices. Aging adds filter drift and noise.
  • Polyphony and unison. Set the voice count from one to sixteen for chords, or stack voices on a single note. Add portamento to glide between notes.
  • Performance controls. Set velocity response, play with pitch bend and modulation, and automate synthesis controls in your DAW.
Workflow

Presets and session recall.

Browse the plug-in's factory bank or choose INIT to build a patch from scratch. Hover a control for help, then save your DAW project or a host preset to keep the complete setup.

The Rack Extension uses Reason's patch browser and a separate bank of original Protocodus sounds. Both versions offer quality settings to balance CPU use and oversampling.

Rack Extension: Reason 14 or later.

Physically modelled taiko

Taikor

Play four physically modelled taiko drums from a 4 by 4 keyboard grid, no keyswitches. Taikor solves every stroke from a struck circular membrane rather than replaying a recording.

Get for free or buy

Name your price on Gumroad. Downloads are not yet available.

Inside the drums

A 4 by 4 grid,
and nothing else.

No keyswitches and no articulation menu. Sixteen notes, and every other key on the keyboard is silent.

  • Sixteen notes, no keyswitches. The octave picks the drum and the bottom four semitones pick the stroke: Don, Ka, Tsu and Don Rim. Every other key on the keyboard stays silent.
  • Four distinct drums. Ō-daiko, chū-daiko, okedo-daiko and shime-daiko each carry their own diameter, body depth, hide and shell, from a 150 cm ō-daiko down to a 30 cm shime.
  • Velocity is stick speed. MIDI velocity sets the impact speed of the bachi, so a harder stroke comes out shorter and brighter as well as louder, not just louder.
  • Damping, bend and placement. Hold CC1 to lay a palm on the head and mute the ring, use the pitch wheel to bend a stroke that is already sounding, and CC16/17 to place each hit around and across the head.
  • No samples. Every stroke is solved from a struck circular membrane in real time, never replayed from a recording.
Workflow

Kits and session recall.

The Drum Layout switch chooses what a keyboard row plays: one head retuned across the rows, or the four family members at their own sizes.

Save the kit as a DAW project or host preset to recall drum sizing, layout and every playing control exactly as you left them.
